jm3cbb-e29714.summary: The third question asks what generates a habit. Mair answers that habits are generated by an act or acts, since repeated acts leave a lasting readiness and memory. Against those who require many acts, he argues that every act, however weak, generates some habit in a well-disposed subject. No fixed number of acts can be specified, a weak cause yields a proportionally weak effect, and every quality of the same lowest species as a habit is itself a habit. Along the way he criticizes the analogy of dripping water hollowing a stone and reinterprets it as an accumulation of imperceptible removals. He then sets out exceptions and hard cases. Intuitive cognition produces no habit, because it naturally requires the object's presence, and neither does a volition caused by intuitive cognition, so beatific enjoyment generates no habit. Against Aquinas, he holds that acts proceeding from infused charity, faith, and hope do generate acquired habits, so that one act can come from two specifically distinct habits. Minor objections, about the habitually intemperate, the swallow that does not make a spring, motion toward virtues, and the hermit's virtues, are resolved.
claims: Habits are generated by an act or acts.
Every act, however weak, generates some habit in a well-disposed subject.
No fixed number of acts can be specified as necessary for a habit.
A weaker cause of the same kind produces a proportionally weaker effect of the same species, except in the special case of judgments.
Whatever is of the same lowest species as a habit is a habit.
Intuitive cognition generates no habit, because it naturally requires the object to be present.
Acts of the will caused by intuitive cognition generate no habit, so beatific enjoyment produces none.
Against Aquinas, acts from infused habits such as charity generate acquired habits.
The same numerical act can be produced by two specifically distinct habits, one infused and one acquired.

jm3cbb-e29714-d1e104.summary: Statement of the third question: from what a habit is generated.

jm3cbb-e29714-d1e111.summary: Mair's conclusion: a habit is generated from an act or acts. After eliciting acts, one finds oneself readier to act, so something remains that prompts this. If one has often seen an object, one easily remembers it, which would be impossible if nothing remained.
claims: A habit is generated from an act or acts.
The readiness and memory that follow acts show that something lasting remains in the agent.

jm3cbb-e29714-d1e131.summary: First objection: if every act generates a habit, then an act elicited with infinitesimal weakness would produce an infinitely small habit, which is absurd.
claims: (Objection) If every act generates a habit, infinitely small habits would result.

jm3cbb-e29714-d1e143.summary: Second objection: such a weak quality would be easily removed, and so would be a disposition rather than a habit, since the two are distinguished by whether they are easily or hardly removed from their subject.
claims: (Objection) A disposition is easily removed from its subject, while a habit is removed only with difficulty.
(Objection) A weak quality from a single weak act is a disposition, not a habit.

jm3cbb-e29714-d1e156.summary: Mair reports the view that a habit requires many acts and argues against it. No definite number of acts can be specified. One intense act produces as much as three or four weak acts that together can produce a habit. By the principle that causes differing only in magnitude produce effects differing only in magnitude, if an intense act produces a large habit then a weak act produces a small one. This holds where no resistance exceeds or equals the agent's activity, as here. Judgments are an exception: an intense intuitive cognition of nearby Socrates causes the judgment 'this is a man', but a weak one from afar does not, and a weaker cognition yields a less perfect judgment of a different species (referring to III, d.2). Cognition and the power produce the judgment, and object and power produce the cognition.
claims: No fixed number of acts required to generate a habit can be specified.
An intense act can equal several weak ones in causal effect.
Causes of the same kind that differ in magnitude produce effects of the same kind that differ in magnitude, absent prevailing resistance.
Judgments are an exception: a weaker cognition yields a judgment of a different species, not a weaker judgment of the same species.
The object's existence is not required for producing a judgment.

jm3cbb-e29714-d1e232.summary: A further argument: the first weak act either produces something or nothing. If something, it is of the same lowest species as a habit and therefore a habit, just as any quality of the same species as heat is heat, and since every part of a habit is a habit, it remains a habit apart from the whole. The opponent may answer with the analogy of dripping water: the first drop does not hollow the stone, but eventually one drop, by its own force and that of the preceding drops, hollows it, so a series of weak acts may finally yield a habit.
claims: Any quality of the same lowest species as a habit is a habit.
Every part of a habit is a habit.
(Opponent) Weak acts may contribute nothing individually until a final act completes the habit, as with dripping water.

jm3cbb-e29714-d1e267.summary: Mair attacks the dripping-water analogy. If the first drop removes nothing, and no later drop is greater than the first, then the eighth or tenth removes nothing either. Appeal to 'the power of the preceding drops' fails, since those drops no longer exist and cannot cooperate.
claims: If the first of equal drops removes nothing, no later drop removes anything either.
Past drops, no longer existing, cannot cooperate in the hollowing.

jm3cbb-e29714-d1e289.summary: Possible rejoinder: although past drops no longer exist, they disposed the stone by softening it, so the last drop can remove something, as a first drop falling on mud of little resistance would.
claims: (Opponent) Earlier drops dispose the stone by softening it, allowing a later drop to hollow it.

jm3cbb-e29714-d1e302.summary: Rebuttal of the softening rejoinder. The stone does not appear softer at the hollow than nearby. An iron ring worn away by daily use, as the saying goes, neither melts nor grows softer.
claims: Hollowing by repeated contact occurs without any softening of the material.

jm3cbb-e29714-d1e316.summary: Even granting the analogy, it does not help the opponent's main point. Every act is by nature generative of habit and the patient is well disposed, so every act generates something in it, and nothing but a habit. Whatever else the act produces, so long as it generates a habit, Mair's thesis stands.
claims: Every act is by its nature generative of habit.
An act acting on a well-disposed patient generates something, namely a habit.

jm3cbb-e29714-d1e332.summary: Confirmation by proportional division. If act a, intense as eight, produces habit b, intense as eight, then half of a produces half of b, one degree of a produces one degree of b, and any part of a, however small, produces a corresponding part of the habit. Whatever a part produces within the whole it produces outside the whole, in a patient without a contrary and supremely disposed.
claims: A part of an act produces a proportional part of the habit.
What a part of a cause produces within the whole, it produces apart from the whole when the patient is well disposed and has no contrary.

jm3cbb-e29714-d1e356.summary: Mair's settled position. One could stubbornly fight over terms by requiring some fixed degree of intensity before calling a quality a habit and calling weaker products dispositions. It is more reasonable to say that whatever is of the same lowest species as a habit is a habit, and that every act, however small, generates a habit in a disposed patient. What is a disposition, easily corrupted and specifically different from habit, is the act itself.
claims: Requiring a threshold intensity for a habit is merely a dispute about terms.
Whatever shares the lowest species of a habit is a habit.
Every act, however small, generates a habit in a disposed patient.
The act is a disposition, easily corrupted and specifically distinct from the habit.

jm3cbb-e29714-d1e380.summary: Objection from Aristotle's Categories: a habit is hard to corrupt, but such a small quality is easily corrupted, so it is not a habit.
claims: (Objection) Being hard to corrupt belongs to habit, and a minimal quality lacks it.

jm3cbb-e29714-d1e389.summary: Reply: the minor premise is denied, with fuller treatment promised under the corruption of habits. On the drops example: even if many drops dispose the stone by softening and the last one hollows it by the power of the earlier ones, this does not help the opponent, because here the patient is already disposed.
claims: It is denied that a small habit is easily corrupted.
The softening version of the drops analogy does not apply where the patient is already well disposed.

jm3cbb-e29714-d1e407.summary: A better account of the drops example and the answer to the first objection. Each drop, by its impetus, removes an imperceptible part of the hard stone, and after ten or twelve drops the removal becomes perceptible and is called hollowing. Similarly, not every slight depression of the nose makes a man snub-nosed, only a notable one. Returning to the original argument, Mair grants that an infinitely small habit can be generated, provided none of it is produced in an instant but the whole at once.
claims: Each drop removes an imperceptible amount, and 'hollowing' names only a perceptible accumulated removal.
Terms like 'hollowing' and 'snub-nosed' apply only past a perceptible threshold.
An infinitely small habit can be generated.

jm3cbb-e29714-d1e439.summary: Second argument against the conclusion: some act produces no habit, so (there being no more reason for one act than another) no act does. Intuitive cognition of Socrates or of whiteness produces no habit, since every habit produced by an act produces an act of the same lowest species as the one it came from, but such a habit together with the power cannot produce intuitive cognition when the object is absent.
claims: (Objection) Intuitive cognition produces no habit.
Every habit produced by an act inclines to acts of the same lowest species as its source.
Habit and power cannot produce intuitive cognition without the object present.

jm3cbb-e29714-d1e472.summary: Third argument: love of God does not cause a habit of love, nor does an act of believing cause a habit of believing, so not every vital act produces a habit. Otherwise two specifically distinct habits (infused and acquired) would immediately produce numerically the same act, which is unfitting, since infused charity immediately inclines to actual love of God and any habit generated from that act would incline to similar acts.
claims: (Objection) Acts of infused virtues such as charity and faith generate no habits.
(Objection) Two specifically distinct habits should not immediately produce numerically the same act.

jm3cbb-e29714-d1e494.summary: Reply to the second argument. Mair grants that intuitive cognition produces no habit; only the accompanying abstractive cognition does. The alternative, that a habit need not incline to an act like its source, is no less awkward, given the more common and (he thinks) truer view that every intuitive cognition differs specifically from every abstractive one. Since intuitive cognition can naturally be had only of a present object, a power to produce a habit would be useless in it, and God and nature do nothing in vain. Habits are given to creatures so they can recall acts and objects when the objects are absent; a habit supplements the power in the object's absence.
claims: Intuitive cognition produces no habit; the accompanying abstractive cognition does.
Every intuitive cognition differs specifically from every abstractive cognition.
A habit-generating power in intuitive cognition would be pointless, and nature does nothing in vain.
Habits exist so that creatures can recall and act toward absent objects.

jm3cbb-e29714-d1e540.summary: Objection to the reply: it would follow that some act of will produces no habit, namely the act caused by and dependent on intuitive cognition. If it were of the same lowest species as a volition caused by abstractive cognition, enjoyment in this life and in heaven would be of the same species, making wayfarer enjoyment beatific. Since this volition cannot exist without the object's presence (even if the object does not cause it directly), by the same reasoning it generates no habit.
claims: (Objection) A volition caused by intuitive cognition cannot exist without the object present and so would generate no habit.
Volitions caused by intuitive and abstractive cognitions must differ in species, or else earthly enjoyment would be beatific.

jm3cbb-e29714-d1e575.summary: Mair accepts the conclusion. A free act of will caused by intuitive cognition causes a further act of will to which the will is purely passive. After loving an intuitively known object one is readier to love, but the habit comes not from the 'intuitive love' (love presupposing intuitive cognition) but from an abstractive love produced in the will. So beatific enjoyment in heaven generates no habit, and Paul after his rapture had no habit able to produce beatific love, only a habit for abstractive love.
claims: A volition caused by intuitive cognition generates no habit directly.
Such a free volition causes another volition, abstractive in kind, toward which the will is passive, and that one generates the habit.
Beatific enjoyment generates no habit.
After his rapture, Paul retained only a habit productive of abstractive love.

jm3cbb-e29714-d1e617.summary: On the third argument, Mair reports Aquinas (ST I-II q.51 a.4 ad 3): acts proceeding from infused habits do not cause a new habit but strengthen the existing one, as medicine given to a healthy person does not cause health but strengthens it.
claims: (Aquinas) Acts from infused habits confirm the existing habit rather than causing a new one.

jm3cbb-e29714-d1e636.summary: Against Aquinas's view: its only reason would be to avoid two habits of the same species in one subject, but there is nothing wrong with two accidents of the same species in the same subject, as with the many memory habits and species in the intellect for objects of the same species. And the problem does not arise here anyway, since acquired and infused charity differ in species.
claims: Two accidents of the same species can coexist in the same subject.
Acquired and infused charity differ in species.

jm3cbb-e29714-d1e660.summary: A further argument: an unbeliever such as Socrates, without infused charity and in original and mortal sin, can still love God, and that act generates a habit. So it does so in Plato, who has charity. Likewise, of two people, one in mortal sin and one in grace, who both will that God be the highest good, if a habit is generated in one it is generated in the other. Otherwise infused charity would block the generation of an unrelated habit.
claims: One without infused charity can love God and thereby acquire a habit.
Having infused charity does not prevent the same act from generating an acquired habit.

jm3cbb-e29714-d1e684.summary: More arguments and Mair's resolution. Ethics II teaches that habits arise from acts, which should not be denied of any act without clear evidence. Aquinas's view would eliminate acquired charity and acquired faith, against the common school. It would deprive one who loves God of a natural aid that one who loves Socrates has. An unbeliever acquires a habit of unbelief by assenting against an article of faith, so a believer acquires a habit by assenting to what is believable. When a converted unbeliever's act of faith destroys the habit of unbelief, it does so only by generating something, since an agent corrupts only by generating. Mair holds that acts of charitable love of God, and of faith and hope, generate habits, and that one numerical act can be produced by two specifically distinct habits, one infused and one naturally acquired.
claims: Acts of charitable love of God, faith, and hope generate acquired habits.
An agent corrupts something only by generating something incompatible with it.
There are acquired charity and acquired faith, in agreement with the common school.
One numerical act can be produced by two specifically distinct habits, infused and acquired.

jm3cbb-e29714-d1e732.summary: Fourth argument: if Socrates is habitually intemperate, an opposite act of temperance generates nothing in him, so not every act generates a habit.
claims: (Objection) An act contrary to an entrenched habit generates no habit.

jm3cbb-e29714-d1e743.summary: Fifth argument: one swallow does not make a spring, nor one day (Ethics I), so one act does not generate a habit.
claims: (Objection) A single act does not suffice for a habit.

jm3cbb-e29714-d1e750.summary: Reply to the fourth argument: the antecedent is granted, because in that case the patient is not well disposed.
claims: An act may fail to generate a habit when the patient is not well disposed, as with someone opposed by a contrary habit.

jm3cbb-e29714-d1e758.summary: Reply to the fifth argument: Aristotle is speaking about the happy person, whom a short time does not make, not about virtue.
claims: Aristotle's swallow saying concerns happiness, not the generation of virtue.

jm3cbb-e29714-d1e765.summary: Sixth argument: if habits are generated from acts, there would be motion per se toward virtues and vices, against Physics V.
claims: (Objection) Generating habits from acts would imply motion per se in the category of quality toward virtue, contrary to Aristotle.

jm3cbb-e29714-d1e772.summary: Reply: according to the Commentator (Averroes), Aristotle there speaks according to the opinion of philosophers who denied that a habit is a virtue until it reaches its highest degree, which is merely a dispute about terms.
claims: Aristotle's denial of motion toward virtues reflects a view that 'virtue' names only a habit at its highest degree.
That disagreement is merely terminological.

jm3cbb-e29714-d1e785.summary: Seventh argument: it follows that habits can be generated from interior acts alone, so a hermit could be magnificent, liberal, magnanimous, and brave.
claims: (Objection) If interior acts suffice for habits, a hermit could have the social virtues.

jm3cbb-e29714-d1e794.summary: Reply: the difficulty is irrelevant to the conclusion, but Mair grants it if the hermit studiously produces the acts of those virtues within himself. He closes by restating that habits are generated from one act or several, as in the proverb that by forging we become smiths.
claims: A hermit can acquire virtues such as liberality by producing their interior acts.
Habits are generated from one act or several.
